title: Given an array of integers, find the maximum absolute value of the sum of any contiguous non-empty subarray. Solve it by running both maximum and minimum Kadane simultaneously and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Maximum Absolute Sum of Any Subarray

s1_definition.profdef: The maximum absolute sum problem asks for the largest absolute value among the sums of all contiguous non-empty subarrays. Because an absolute value is large when the underlying sum is either very positive or very negative, the problem reduces to running Kadane's algorithm twice in the same pass, once to find the maximum subarray sum and once to find the minimum subarray sum, and returning the larger of the maximum and the absolute value of the minimum.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a sequence of daily net cash swings for an account and wants the single most extreme continuous swing in either direction, whether it is the biggest continuous inflow or the biggest continuous outflow, because both represent large liquidity events. He simultaneously hunts for the most positive run and the most negative run, and the headline number is whichever has the larger magnitude.
s1_definition.oneliner: The largest absolute subarray sum is the bigger of the maximum subarray sum and the magnitude of the minimum subarray sum.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The maximum absolute sum problem asks for the largest absolute value among the sums of all contiguous non-empty subarrays. Because an absolute value is large when the underlying sum is either very positive or very negative, the problem reduces to running Kadane's algorithm twice in the same pass, once to find the maximum subarray sum and once to find the minimum subarray sum, and returning the larger of the maximum and the absolute value of the minimum.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a sequence of daily net cash swings for an account and wants the single most extreme continuous swing in either direction, whether it is the biggest continuous inflow or the biggest continuous outflow, because both represent large liquidity events. He simultaneously hunts for the most positive run and the most negative run, and the headline number is whichever has the larger magnitude.

**One line to remember:** The largest absolute subarray sum is the bigger of the maximum subarray sum and the magnitude of the minimum subarray sum.

sections.s2_technical:
The absolute value of a subarray sum is large in two distinct situations: when the sum itself is a large positive number, or when the sum is a large negative number whose magnitude is big. There is no single Kadane pass that directly maximizes absolute value, because absolute value is not linear, but we can decompose the problem cleanly. The maximum absolute subarray sum equals the maximum over two quantities: the maximum subarray sum and the absolute value of the minimum subarray sum.

So we run both variants of Kadane at once in a single loop. We keep a running maximum and a global maximum exactly as in standard Kadane, and simultaneously a running minimum and a global minimum exactly as in minimum Kadane. For each element we update `curMax = Math.max(nums[i], curMax + nums[i])` and `curMin = Math.min(nums[i], curMin + nums[i])`, then refresh both globals. At the end the answer is `Math.max(globalMax, Math.abs(globalMin))`.

An elegant alternative that senior engineers often cite uses prefix sums: the maximum absolute subarray sum equals the maximum prefix sum minus the minimum prefix sum over the running prefix totals, including an implicit zero prefix at the start. This works because any subarray sum is a difference of two prefix sums, and the largest magnitude difference comes from pairing the highest prefix with the lowest. The senior-level nuance is recognizing that absolute-value objectives usually split into a maximize branch and a minimize branch, and that both the dual-Kadane and the prefix-sum formulations capture this.

We seed carefully from the first element to keep the subarray non-empty, just as in the individual Kadane variants. The time complexity is linear, O(n), a single pass whether we use dual Kadane or prefix sums, and the space complexity is O(1). This decomposition is the clean, expected solution and demonstrates comfort combining two known algorithms into one pass.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the liquidity-monitoring team tracks a sequence of daily net cash swings for an account, positive on net inflow days and negative on net outflow days. For regulatory liquidity-event reporting they must report the single most extreme continuous cash swing in magnitude, regardless of direction, because both a very large continuous inflow and a very large continuous outflow are material liquidity events that must be flagged. This is exactly the maximum absolute sum of any subarray problem.

Problem 2 — Scanning every possible run of days for its absolute sum by brute force is quadratic and does not scale across the bank's accounts and histories. Running both maximum and minimum Kadane in a single linear pass and taking the larger magnitude gives the answer in one scan per account, which makes the nightly liquidity-event report feasible.

The code has the shared `Account` class, an `ExtremeSwingAnalyzer` service with a `largestAbsoluteSwing` method running dual Kadane, and a runnable `MaxAbsoluteSumDemo` main class that runs Rajesh's and Priya's cash-swing sequences, logging both running states at fine level and the extreme swing at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's swings are 1, -3, 2, 3, -4. We seed the running maximum, global maximum, running minimum, and global minimum all at the first element, 1.

Step 1 at index 1, value -3: running maximum becomes the larger of -3 and 1 plus -3 which is -2, so -2. Running minimum becomes the smaller of -3 and 1 plus -3 which is -2, so -3. Global maximum stays 1, global minimum becomes -3.

Step 2 at index 2, value 2: running maximum becomes the larger of 2 and -2 plus 2 which is 0, so 2. Running minimum becomes the smaller of 2 and -3 plus 2 which is -1, so -1. Global maximum becomes 2, global minimum stays -3.

Step 3 at index 3, value 3: running maximum becomes the larger of 3 and 2 plus 3 which is 5, so 5. Running minimum becomes the smaller of 3 and -1 plus 3 which is 2, so 2. Global maximum becomes 5, global minimum stays -3.

Step 4 at index 4, value -4: running maximum becomes the larger of -4 and 5 plus -4 which is 1, so 1. Running minimum becomes the smaller of -4 and 2 plus -4 which is -2, so -4. Global maximum stays 5, global minimum becomes -4.

At the end the global maximum is 5 and the global minimum is -4, so the answer is the larger of 5 and the absolute value of -4 which is 4, giving 5. The most extreme swing for Rajesh is a positive run of 5, the subarray 2 followed by 3.

```
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Rajesh Kumar (SAV2001) swings
2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Day 3: curMax=5 curMin=2
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Largest absolute swing over [1, -3, 2, 3, -4] = max(5, |-4|) = 5
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Rajesh Kumar largest absolute swing = 5
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Priya Sharma (CUR3001) swings
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Largest absolute swing over [2, -5, -3, 1] = max(2, |-8|) = 8
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Priya Sharma largest absolute swing = 8
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: swings [1,-3,2,3,-4]
    │
    ▼
  ExtremeSwingAnalyzer.largestAbsoluteSwing()  (dual Kadane, one pass)
    │ seed: curMax=gMax=1, curMin=gMin=1
    │
    ├─ i=1 -3: curMax=-2 curMin=-3  gMax1  gMin-3
    ├─ i=2  2: curMax=2  curMin=-1  gMax2  gMin-3
    ├─ i=3  3: curMax=5  curMin=2   gMax5  gMin-3 ← max run
    └─ i=4 -4: curMax=1  curMin=-4  gMax5  gMin-4
    │
    ▼
  answer = max(gMax 5, |gMin -4| = 4) = 5
    │
    ▼
  Output: 5  (most extreme continuous swing, a positive run 2+3)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The maximum absolute sum of any subarray asks for the largest absolute value among the sums of all contiguous non-empty subarrays, and I solve it in a single linear pass. The key observation is that an absolute sum is large in two distinct ways: when the sum is a large positive number, or when the sum is a large negative number whose magnitude is big. Since absolute value is not linear, I decompose the objective into two Kadane problems, finding the maximum subarray sum and the minimum subarray sum, and the answer is the larger of the maximum and the absolute value of the minimum.

I run both variants of Kadane together in one loop, keeping a running maximum and global maximum alongside a running minimum and global minimum, updating all four per element. An elegant alternative I like to mention uses prefix sums, where the maximum absolute subarray sum equals the maximum prefix total minus the minimum prefix total including an implicit zero at the start, because every subarray sum is a difference of two prefix sums and the largest magnitude difference pairs the highest prefix with the lowest.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the liquidity-monitoring team. We tracked daily net cash swings for an account, positive on inflow days and negative on outflow days, and for regulatory liquidity-event reporting we had to report the single most extreme continuous swing in magnitude regardless of direction, because both a very large continuous inflow and a very large continuous outflow were material events. Running dual Kadane in one pass gave that extreme in a single scan per account, scaling across the bank's histories in the nightly report.

The senior-level point I make is that absolute-value objectives almost always split into a maximize branch and a minimize branch, and recognizing that lets me reuse two algorithms I already know instead of inventing a bespoke one. I also mention the prefix-sum formulation as a second valid lens, which signals flexibility, and that for monetary values I accumulate in a long or BigDecimal to avoid overflow across long histories. Offering both the dual-Kadane and prefix-sum views, plus the overflow safeguard, is what tells an interviewer I understand the problem deeply rather than reciting one pattern.
